Temperature and humidity: Climate control is inconsistent and often uncomfortable. During warmer months, the office can feel excessively warm and humid - even damp. Workstation ergonomics and maintenance: Adjustable desks frequently do not raise or lower as intended, and chairs are often damaged or malfunctioning, including seats that tilt unexpectedly or have torn upholstery. Capsule rooms: These rooms are difficult to reserve, and when available, technology is frequently unreliable. Monitors and audio equipment do not consistently function, limiting their usefulness for meetings and focused work. Phone booths: Ventilation and temperature control are inconsistent, particularly when the fans are not functioning. Additionally, the oversized monitors take up considerable space and are positioned in a way that makes it difficult to use a laptop and external monitor simultaneously. An open laptop often obstructs the lower portion of the monitor, creating an inefficient workspace. Collectively, these issues make it difficult to maintain a comfortable, functional, and productive work environment. Improvements to lighting, climate control, workstation maintenance, and the reliability and ergonomic design of shared workspaces would significantly improve the PulsePoint experience.

I really enjoy our PulsePoint location! The building is clean, well-maintained, and a great place to work. However, the parking process is one area that could be improved. **Morning arrival (8 steps):** 1. Park in a visitor space. 2. Enter the building and swipe in. 3. Go upstairs to the second floor. 4. Sign out a physical parking pass. 5. Go downstairs and return to my car. 6. Drive 2 minutes past empty spaces to the satellite lot. 7. Park and display the pass. 8. Walk 4 minutes back to the building. **End of day (7 steps):** 1. Walk 4 minutes to the satellite lot. 2. Drive 2 minutes back to the main lot. 3. Park in a visitor space. 4. Reenter the building. 5. Go upstairs to return the pass. 6. Go downstairs to my car. 7. Leave for the day. That's **15 steps and at least 12 minutes of unnecessary walking and driving per visit**, excluding the time spent entering the building and managing the pass. I understand there are parking and building constraints, and our PulsePoint manager does an excellent job working within them. My concern is with the process, not the people managing it. Could we explore allowing employees to keep physical passes longer, moving pass pickup closer to the entrance, or utilizing available spaces in the main lot? Even small changes could eliminate unnecessary steps and meaningfully improve the employee experience at an otherwise great location.

Many of the physical features of my PulsePoint location are the same factors that limit my ability to work effectively. At this point, I’m not sure what changes could realistically be made that would make regular office attendance and the broader hybrid model worth the cost and disruption. The lighting is extremely bright, and I frequently leave the office with a significant headache. The phone booths are not a viable option for me  they feel claustrophobic, and when they are used, they are often occupied by the same individuals for most of the day. That reduces availability for the impromptu calls and quick discussions they are intended to support. Adding more booths does not feel like the right solution either—many associates avoid them due to discomfort, including. Conference room availability and functionality is also inconsistent. Some rooms lack screens or the setup needed to support multiple people joining the same meeting effectively. As a result, teams often end up taking meetings from the floor, where overlapping conversations create significant background noise and regularly lead to complaints that I’m difficult to hear. In addition, the rooms do not provide reliable privacy  walls are thin and conversations carry between rooms, which undermines the purpose of reserving a room in the first place. Other office amenities are not strong differentiators for me. While fitness equipment may be helpful for some, it does not offset the time and schedule impact of commuting overall, I have been able to work out less since returning to the office. The café and cafeteria are workable, but cleanliness is inconsistent, healthy options are limited, and the pricing is difficult to justify given the increased cost of commuting and attending in person. Finally, the desk and workspace model creates added friction. Frequently changing desks and setups means repeatedly adjusting settings, moving equipment, and dealing with connectivity or configuration issues.

comment: As a people manager, the requirement to be in the office three days a week presents significant challenges when there is no dedicated office or private workspace available. A large part of my role involves coaching, mentoring, providing feedback, addressing sensitive employee matters, and participating in meetings that require confidentiality and discretion. Working in an open space makes these responsibilities difficult. Conversations can easily be overheard, colleagues frequently walk by and can see information on computer screens, and there is limited opportunity to speak openly during meetings without disturbing others or compromising privacy. While I understand the importance of in-office collaboration, the current workspace setup does not adequately support the responsibilities of people leaders. It can actually make it harder to connect meaningfully with team members, conduct effective coaching sessions, and participate fully in discussions. If managers are expected to be in the office three days a week, there should be appropriate private spaces available to perform our responsibilities effectively. Providing access to dedicated offices or reliable private meeting spaces would help create a more productive, professional, and confidential environment for both managers and their teams.

The hybrid offices significantly improve my ability to facilitate Virtual Instructor-Led Training (VILT) because they provide the dual-monitor setup I need to manage training materials and learner engagement effectively. However, the two-hour reservation limit makes these spaces impractical for facilitating training sessions that typically extend beyond that timeframe. While meeting and huddle rooms provide some privacy and can serve as alternatives when necessary, their technology setup is less conducive to VILT. Using my laptop alongside the room's display screen does not provide the same functionality or flexibility as a dedicated dual-monitor workstation. When facilitating, I need to display training content, facilitator guides, and training notes on one monitor while keeping the virtual classroom visible on the other. This allows me to monitor learners' reactions, follow chat discussions, respond to questions, and adjust my facilitation in real time without constantly switching between windows. Having access to a private workspace equipped with dual monitors for the full duration of a training session would significantly improve my experience. Extending the hybrid office reservation limit for employees facilitating VILT would be especially beneficial, as it would support both effective training delivery and learner engagement.

Overall, my PulsePoint experience has reinforced that physical presence does not automatically translate into better collaboration, engagement, or productivity. Requiring employees to commute, transport equipment, and work in a less comfortable environment adds unnecessary time, expense, and logistical challenges without a clear operational benefit. With schedules, breaks, and lunches strictly controlled by WFM, there is limited flexibility for meaningful in-person interaction, which raises questions about the actual value of onsite attendance. Working remotely allows me to maintain a more comfortable, consistent, and productive environment while eliminating unnecessary commuting and its associated environmental impact. If onsite attendance is intended to foster collaboration, there should be intentional opportunities to collaborate and measurable benefits that justify the requirement. Simply occupying the same building while continuing to perform independent, computer-based work does not accomplish that objective. I would encourage leadership to evaluate the PulsePoint experience based on actual productivity, employee feedback, operational outcomes, and meaningful collaboration rather than physical attendance. Greater remote-work flexibility would demonstrate a commitment to employee well-being, efficiency, environmental responsibility, and results-driven performance.

Overall, I find the PulsePoint experience disappointing. On the days I'm in the office, there are often very few people there, and those who are present typically aren't the colleagues I work with or collaborate with regularly. While it's nice to see a familiar face, it doesn't meaningfully improve collaboration or connection with my team, which is spread across the country. For a company with a geographically dispersed workforce that emphasizes culture, innovation, and forward thinking, mandated # of times in the office and days of the week feels disconnected from how many of us actually work. No matter how much we invest in improving the physical PulsePoint spaces, I don't think those changes will address the underlying frustration with a mandate that doesn't necessarily align with employees' roles, teams, or ways of working. I believe there is an opportunity to rethink what meaningful workplace flexibility and collaboration look like rather than equating physical presence with engagement or productivity. In my experience, the mandate has created frustration without delivering the sense of connection or collaboration it was intended to foster. I'd love to see the company place greater trust in employees and their leaders to determine when being in the office adds value, rather than applying a one-size-fits-all requirement across such a diverse, geographically distributed workforce.

Ironically, much of the collaboration happening at the PulsePoint is also conducted through virtual meetings, with employees sitting close to one another and participating in separate calls. This creates a noisy and distracting environment where people frequently interrupt one another's concentration. I find that I can work more comfortably, efficiently, and with fewer distractions from home. I would appreciate greater flexibility in office attendance, particularly for employees whose responsibilities and collaboration are primarily virtual. comment: The wide-open desk space can be very distracting and makes it difficult to maintain focus and productivity. When desks were assigned, there was more separation between workspaces, which provided a better environment for both meetings and focused work. Without that separation, I find that my productivity is significantly higher when working from home. The focus rooms help, but availability and reservation restrictions make them difficult to rely on. They are often fully reserved, and the two-hour limit is not practical on days with multiple meetings. Additionally, because reservations are limited to one per day, employees with meetings at different times cannot reserve a focus room for each meeting. More flexibility in both the workspace setup and focus-room reservation policy would make the office much more conducive to productive work.

From my perspective, the question is not whether I am willing to come into an office. I absolutely would when there is a meaningful business reason to be onsite. My request is for flexibility when there is not an in-person business need. For example, I would be very willing to come onsite for leadership meetings, planning sessions, training, team events, or other activities where face-to-face interaction adds value. What I’m asking for is consideration of a primarily remote arrangement based on the nature of my role and team structure, rather than a three-day/wk onsite requirement. I believe that arrangement would allow me to maximize productivity, maintain confidentiality, and remain fully accessible to my nationally distributed team while still being available onsite when there is a meaningful business need.

It's a very sterile environment that can feel more uncomfortable and transactional than most and I often end up with a headache from the office lighting/screen/keyboard arrangement. Many people are very loud and disruptive. It's hard to work when there's 14 different video calls surrounding you, and I really wish people wouldn't go in sick. It is often a nice change of scenery, and i don't overall mind it. But it's not a useful place for me to work on most days and results in lost time and productive, as well as a selection of work that makes sense from that public location The lack of phyical firewall and that I don't think people stay in assigned areas concerns me from a compliance standpoint.

comment: Coming to a pulse point to connect virtually with others is a waste of my time and gas. It's about a 45 drive one way, to do the same things I do at home.

Hard to find a location in the office to focus and concentrate. Seems associates that take back-to-back calls are spread throughout all the sections of the building. I take a few meetings and always try to get in a huddle/meeting room when possible.
vending machines very expensive so lower cost or adding complimentary healthy fruits/snacks would be great
No, it is good. Thanks

There is almost no collaboration between individuals, so it is not achieving the in-person collaboration the business expects because everyone reporting to this Pulse Point has very very different roles that do not overlap in any way.
Compared to where I've worked in the past, this office is very blah.
I feel that the company would better support me by allowing me to be fully remote. There would be less disruption to my work and my physical well being.
Not at this time.

My overall experience in the office is not bad, but it feels less productive at times compared to working in my home office. The spaces are generic to accommodate any associate and may not have an ergonomic keyboard or even a mouse available. Not all spaces have two screens, some only have one, which no one wants to use if two screens are an option. Going into the office is not needed for me to do my job, or to do my job well. While in the office, I’ll end up on calls for meetings and collaboration because the people I work with may not be in the same office as me or there at the same time. Days like that I could have done those calls/meetings from home without having the commute, extra distractions of others in the office and sometimes expenses/time added that is associated with having to go into the office. These days, in the office, it is more distracting than working from home. Due to the fact the spaces are so open and walls so low, others collaborating in open spaces can be distracting and more noticeable than it was pre-pandemic when there was a different floor plan design and spaces with more separation (higher walls or work areas by teams). I find the white noise pumped into the office space distracting. The in-office experience can be good if the people you need to work with are there at the same time and if there are no system or laptop issues. I do enjoy the hybrid work experience because it gives an opportunity to see others in person when needed, but it also allows for flexibility to work from home. I really enjoy working from home and having less distractions around me. I feel like WFH is a benefit to my productivity and work happiness in ways I did not expect prior to the pandemic forcing us to work from home.

I think the PULSE Point concept is ridiculous. There are certain functions that simply do not require coming together except for largest meetings  yet our large conference room cannot accommodate all staff. If an individual is required to come in for one, three or five days they should eb required to stay for a minimum of four hours (not a half hour)in which case I think you will find the office footprint is inadequate to accommodate this.

We have a very basic building. Whoever designed it with the open ceiling gave us no sound proofing to prevent hearing conversations (Teams meetings & people collaborating). Since that cannot be changed, we need more conference rooms. We also need better plumbing, better temperature control (I should not have to wear a coat/blanket/gloves & I know this is hard to accommodate all people's preferences) & food.

comment: I would like to see an upgraded Bevi machine, similar to the one at other Pulsepoints!

I want to thank everyone involved in providing a security presence in our parking garage. It’s reassuring to know that our safety is being looked after, and I really appreciate the effort that goes into making that happen. I also want to recognize Kim Akins, Lonnie, and Eric Thomas for staying on top of facilities and security concerns and making sure issues are addressed when they come up. Their hard work and attention to these matters make a difference, and I’m grateful for all they do.
I appreciate the PulsePoint location. I am able to focus on work and help myself to beverages or dine in the cafeteria to take breaks. Great concept and truly appreciative.
I personally do not mind going in but from a managers' perspective it makes Zero sense, all our direct reports are virtual and in different states.

Overall, my experience at PulsePoint has been pleasant, and I appreciate the comfortable, accommodating environment. Aside from technical issues with workstation equipment and display settings that have carried over to my home setup, my primary concern is the value of onsite attendance for my role. As part of a production-based team with colleagues and business partners located nationwide, our work and collaboration are effectively accomplished remotely. I share this feedback in hopes that fully remote arrangements may be considered for roles where productivity, focus, and collaboration are better supported from home.

comment: At the Hanover, MD office we often do not have coffee stir sticks. I get we may not get plastic ware like forks and spoons, but at least we can get stir sticks for coffee.
Would like better selection of drinks/snack/food options on both levels of office where desk are available

Overall I like the look and feel of the office on Russell Road. The couple of things I would point out are having an ice machine in both break rooms, fresh food options and vending in both break rooms.

The commute to this PulsePoint was not covered in the survey and needs to be addressed. I was assigned this PulsePoint because of my reasonable proximity to it but since my route requires the 405 freeway, I end up wasting lots of time throughout my day sitting in traffic during my commute. Additionally, my job does not require spontaneous or scheduled in-person meetings/collaborations, none of my organization's leaders work in this PulsePoint, and generally, other associates take virtual meetings at their desk which creates some noise throughout the day that hinders my ability to focus on my job. Because of these aspects, I lose productivity when I go and work at this PulsePoint.

comment: The current workspace makes it difficult to focus due to ongoing meetings and conversations throughout the area, along with limited use/availability of private spaces for calls.

It would be nice if the hybrid policy was revised to be more fitting to those who could benefit from it more. Crossing state lines and burning through a quarter tank of gas for each round trip to the office, when there aren't any colleagues to see, feels kind of silly. It's a loss of productivity and can be demoralizing at times.

Oftentimes my workstation I reserved is taken by another associate, because they're either not paying attention to the spot they grabbed, or they never reserved a spot in the first place, which causes unnecessary issues. Also, a significant portion of cubicles are saved for those using the cube sharing program. This limits options for associates who are not in that program. I've had to sit in the lunchroom using just my laptop due to no available space. The noise level also gets VERY distracting at times when people in offices are not closing their doors for meetings or when there is a lot of side conversations in the workstation areas.

Hybrid/hotel space does not work for everyone, especially those in director/manager positions and pulse points that share space with ELV/CBH add additional complexities as it relates to firewall/CSI. It is nice that there is a lot of open space, but people are not in the office for open gathering, we are tied to phones/meetings.

For probably 90% of the workforce, going into a PulsePoint makes no sense for our role. I have zero colleagues in my office and commute an hour to do the same exact thing I do at home. There is no collaboration or teamwork happening in our PulsePoint. In today's environment, it is extremely rare to have actual teammates co-located in your city. We are archaic asking our employees to sit in traffic and pay for gas to literally sit alone in a cubicle and talk to no one.

Aside from the convenience of working from home, there are 2 main reasons why I prefer not work from my local PulsePoint too often: 1) The shared spaces are very loud unless I am in a conference room and shut the doors. This prevents me from doing focused work. 2) The workspaces are not always clean. Previous users sometimes leave trash or food behind, which I have to clean first.

comment: Parking lot safety: Last winter, I nearly slipped and fell in the parking lot. I was not injured, but the experience was unsettling. Office distractions: Nearby conversations and foot traffic make it difficult to concentrate and can disrupt provider and virtual meetings. People on the other end of calls have also commented on the background noise. While the low cubicle walls may encourage collaboration, they also increase distractions. Workplace amenities: Our building does not have treadmill desks, so associates cannot try that option. It also lacks hot meals and healthy choices such as fruits and vegetables. I usually bring food, but there are few suitable options if I need something additional. In-person collaboration: I understand that collaboration is a reason for coming into the office. However, meetings are not always held in person, and when conference rooms are unavailable, we often join from our individual desks. That makes the benefit of being onsite less clear. Technology issues: Occasionally, a headset disconnects without warning and audio switches to the computer’s speakers. Until the issue is corrected, others nearby may hear the conversation, which is disruptive and concerning.

comment: If I get promoted, I will have to start coming into the office 3 days a week. I am already less effective on the one day a week I am in the office. Conversations around me are distracting and provide NO benefit, as I do not work with anyone in our PulsePoint. I dread a promotion because I will end up having to put in so much extra work at home to complete my work due to the ineffectiveness of working in the office. I do not mind too much coming in once a week (and it does help build a feeling of connection to the enterprise) but coming in 3 times a week actually makes me not want to get promoted. I am sure I am not the only one who feels this way.  I do understand the benefits of a hybrid model, but it should be more nuanced based on the actual role and WHO the person works with. People who work within a PulsePoint that is largely for one division (For example, Wallingford is largely for people who work on Anthem Connecticut book of business) can have real value from in person collaboration. For those of us working for something not dominant in the building, coming in three days a week is detrimental to our work, not helpful. There is NO benefit for us beyond a few times a month.

comment: Nope they're doing a great job to keep the building running. I'd love to see 2nd monitors at all the stations on 3 but I acknowledge I could just sit somewhere else that does have 2 monitors, I just like the seat I usually sit at and am stubborn.

just as stated before as for a present age where business must capitalize on revenue, the use of Pulsepoints are mismanaged.  if CCRs are local and in same Pulsepoint, then they should be with their manager to help with questions.  Teams are using collab rooms to work together, but other teams are out in cubes.  it should be a more if not all then none approach.  Trainers who are required to come in to teach a virtual session cannot use a collab room to teach as those collab rooms are used by managers or teams as stated above.

I spend a majority of my day on teams calls with associates across the enterprise. Due to this I have to sit in a small capsule to have privacy which can be uncomfortable and cramped. Often the lights turn off and the additional monitor does not work.

Respectfully, I understand the intent of collaboration. I believe it is most beneficial for teams that have a local/onsite present. My team is located across multiple states. My time in the office is spent on calls connecting virtually through MS teams.

I appreciate being able to access this PulsePoint, however I would love at least one more space where I can have confidential meetings and use an additional monitor. There is only one Staff VP office and I can only reserve for 2 hour blocks. There are very few people in this office - sometimes I am the only one there, but I do want to respect others. The only other options are small conference rooms with no monitors.

comment: I like the location. There used to be a cafeteria in our building that closed. New Coffee machine and new water machine seem absolutely necessary. Also it would be nice to have healthier snack options (fresh fruit!!!)

I think it is covered in the other answers made. Previously remote employees regardless of your PulsePoint experience should not need to go in an office. The building is fine, most things work as expected.

Not in relation to the PulsePoint itself, but I believe associates would benefit from a review of hybrid categorization. I am required to be in person 3 times per week which is manageable, but often productivity is hindered in person due to the amount of colleagues present. Collaboration is helpful, but can occasionally be disruptive when it is not controlled. There are a small amount of private offices that can be reserved but it is not feasible to rely on this option ongoing due to the limited number in relation to the amount of associates required to be present on the same cadence due to their hybrid category. I believe that a requirement of 1-2 days would be more effective, with the assumption that prioritization be made to meetings that need to take place in person which could increase the amount of days present but at the associate's discretion.

This PulsePoint is nice in theory, but not many people are on-site, so the collaboration is lacking. Sometimes I feel lonely when I am on-site and end up being the only person in the office, which feels unsafe, especially as a woman. I also live very far from the PulsePoint and would prefer to be fully virtual and just visit when truly necessary to make my time spent commuting more worth it.

It's very frustrating to not have clear, REASONABLE rules around pulse point spaces/hybrid work. Reading the hybrid policy, it does not specify the rules around what constitutes hybrid vs not (time, distance), effectively making it up to the discretion of HR what is required which creates unfair advantages/disadvantages for employees. Further there are not any exceptions made when requested at hire or when management in your dept also requests full-time work at home for an employee if they feel it's appropriate. Why wouldn't it be left up to the discretion of an employee's managers/directors to make the call instead of HR deciding. The fact that the only option available to avoid extreme hybrid policies is to be sick or waste a Drs. time and an employee's money to fill out ADA forms is disappointing and shows a lack of support for employees and their daily work needs. Requiring employees to drive an hour plus each way and put 120 miles on their vehicle creating more wear and tear and heavy costs for fuel doesn't seem reasonable and I feel that Anthem is going to potentially drive away good talent, either that is currently employed, or future employees that would be a valuable asset due to rigid, vague policies, especially when some competitors embrace more work at home opportunities and don't have such rigid rules around it. If an employee is successful in getting work done and creating quality work while working at home, taking away from that just because of a generic policy doesn't make sense. It gives the illusion of control more than support and discourages employees from giving their all.

comment: It would be great if the space was fully carpeted, especially on days with inclement weather.

In my current role I attend all of my meetings virtually. Going into the office does not allow for more collaboration as there is not anyone within the office that relate to my work or could overlap with my work. The requirement to attend the office a certain number of days a month, does not add to the value of my work. Also, my work is not conducive to an open office as topics that are discrete in nature occur and should not be heard on an open floor. This causes me to search and find open office space or move into a capsule, which are not comfortable for someone of my size, for a meeting.
No. I think the office is very nice and has what we need to do our jobs.
Ellis, Brian the team responsible for maintaining the office work really hard.

Having previously W@H associates travel to go to a pulsepoint location is counterproductive. Having to make reservations, not having your own personal space, not having vending and/or food options, not having a clean workspace, being next to people that have different job functions and are loud makes for an uncomfortable work experience. I like to have the comfort of my personal belongings and personal space. The teams I support are located throughout the country. There is no time for impromptu collaboration. Everyone is in meetings and busy. Having to go into the office after many years of being home seems unfair and quite honestly extremely costly. (ie gas, prices, food, travel (time is precious)).

comment: My PulsePoint itself is wonderful and the gym is a great benefit. But it adds very little to my overall work success and probably takes away from it due to added travel time and planning. I rarely have a need to meet with colleagues as most are in other states or other countries. Trips to the office I'm generally finding a quiet place I can work alone as I do at home and join meetings. I also use the gym when I visit.
Going into the office is not necessary for my role and does not enhance my performance. I do not work or interact with anyone at my PulsePoint. I only go in because I have to.
My experience is a good one

Yes, I want to give a shout out to both Shawna Brodie and Frank Osterhout for always doing what they can to ensure we have what we need as associates. They both always go the extra mile, and it's so appreciated.
Thank you for the outreach and consideration to the feedback.

Some roles do not require being in office. I understand wanting to push for collaboration and teamwork but when a particular team is located in different parts of the country it is pointless to be in office all by yourself unless the employee requests to be in office like for example if the associate has an environment at home that causes distractions

I didn't see this mentioned in the survey, but the PARKING in SEATTLE is EXPENSIVE! It would be ideal to have some sort of company rate or discount. It's hourly parking, which affects how long employees actually stay in the office when they do come in. So, if you want employees to stay in the office a full day or at least longer than they do now, implementing a parking subsidy would help that. Reiterating the open workstation floorplan is nice for engagement and collaboration with colleagues but is not good for meetings and phone calls (even if you are not the one making the calls or in a meeting--you hear the others) and it can be distracting. Better options for the lunchroom like non-dairy options for coffee. Also having food options (vending) for snacks would be nice. Having better office supplies like sticky notes, nice pens, nice notebooks, etc. would be helpful, to use in the office and at home as well.

Overall, I enjoy coming to the PulsePoint to collaborate with my team, colleagues and manager. I like the sit/stand desks and the Bevi machine. As a manager I am often in meetings that require discretion or no background noise. This is an everyday occurrence. On busy days it can be quite noisy in the office. I often get comments on calls that they can hear people in background who are on other calls. I need multiple screens which are available at the desk and in focus rooms, but not in the 'pods'. Overall, I do not feel that it is necessary to be in the office 3x/week for me to accomplish my work including collaborating with others. I do feel 1-2x/week would be more appropriate.
Office is not fully open with areas not being used despite the fact that somedays it is hard to make a reservation d/t availability. Then you get to the office and no one is there.

Our office is a restricted-access location, and we often have associates request access or arrive without first reviewing the location details. I think it would be helpful to provide a reminder or communication explaining the difference between open-access and restricted-access PulsePoint locations. Our office is also located in a property-managed building with a separate security checkpoint, so building access and suite access require different processes. While I’d love to arrange building access for everyone who visits, it requires advance coordination and isn’t always possible on short notice. We also have associates arrive without requesting suite access, which means someone has to let them in and out throughout their visit. These may seem like small things, but they can create unnecessary challenges for both visitors and those managing the office. A simple reminder encouraging associates to review the location page, request the appropriate access in advance, and reach out with questions before their visit would go a long way toward making the process smoother for everyone.
I enjoy in-office meetings but the weekly requirement and limited space/tech issues are more of a hindrance. Also cannot accommodate individual ergonomics
My overall pulsepoint experience has been great. The only improvement I would recommend is onsite food options.
Once upon a time, we got free snacks. That has been replaced by a vending machine. We also got free fruit (bananas, oranges, etc.) in the Sears Tower office. We no longer get them.

Being an associate that does not have other team members in the office, if find being mandated to visit a pulse point 3-4 days per week to be very disruptive and has negative impacts to efficiency and my productivity. Having a static setup that does not have to be fiddled with several days away, provides for a better experience and increases productivity. When I work at home, I have zero technological frustrations, and my productivity is higher, as I generally start earlier and work later, as I do not have to spend valuable time commuting during rush hour. Also, when I am in the office, I spend all of my day on Teams meetings collaborating with associates across the county. The extent of my collaboration in the office is limited to a smile as someone passes by your cubicle.

The other members of my team work at other pulse points or work at home because they're not near a pulse point. So, I come into the office three times a week to work remotely. I would rather do that from home if the company would let me.
It is counter-productive for my role to be performed at a Pulsepoint.

I understand there is nothing the enterprise can do about mindful behavior within shared workspaces  however, some associates would benefit from understanding how to adjust voice volume during meetings along with being conscious of information shared during those meetings - at times of a personal nature. It can be difficult to tune out.
I do miss having hot food options in our cafeteria.

At our location specifically, approximately half of the office space is being leased to other organizations, yet information about these tenants is primarily shared informally rather than through official communication. I would appreciate greater transparency regarding which organizations share our building, particularly from a workplace safety and security perspective. While I recognize that badge-controlled access provides a level of security, learning indirectly that we share space with healthcare executives and organizations that have previously been the subject of public protests raises concerns. Given the heightened awareness surrounding workplace safety following the UnitedHealthcare executive shooting, I believe proactive communication about shared tenants, potential security considerations, and existing safety measures would help employees feel more informed and secure in the workplace.
Most, > 95%, of my interactions are virtual with colleagues across the country so being at a pulse point does not enhance that.

For me, the biggest opportunities to improve the PulsePoint experience are noise, cleanliness, and access to food. It can be difficult to concentrate when multiple people are taking calls nearby, and I would like to see more consistent attention to cleanliness. Most importantly, having no cafeteria or other option to purchase a meal or drink in the building is difficult. Having to leave the building and walk to another building for food is especially challenging during the winter.

Going into the office is supposed to be a collaborative resource. However no one, not 1 person, I work with is in my office. I don’t need to talk to or collaborate with others who are not on my team. Quite frankly it’s a waste of time making small talk with people on top of the commute. My biggest issue with our pulse point is that it’s not cleaned nightly. If someone is taking a call longer than 5 minutes from their desk they should be asked to go to a private room or asked to leave. There is no oversight. It’s just a bunch of employees doing whatever they want.

comment: Please do not make us come to the office full time. The hybrid schedule is a nice balance. It takes time out of my day to pack up my stuff and travel to the office when I can just walk into my home office and start working. This collaboration idea and these videos of people standing around a white board with sticky notes and nodding their heads is a myth. It doesn't happen that way. It's a meeting that someone brings up another topic which turns into another meeting to discuss further. And that's fine with me.

I just can't help thinking that I can work more efficiently at home considering that the majority of people I work with aren't in NH. I have to drive 45 (or more) min to sit in a cube focusing on my things or trying not to disturb others while on Teams calls. Ditto trying to tune out others who are on calls. It's been nice to see coworkers from 'back in the day,' but in the end we're there to work, not socialize. I have a quiet workspace at home and easy access to exercise opportunities outside my door.
Overall, I appericate that everyone does there part.

Would like access to alternate types of keyboards/mouse. The current ones have legs that break very easily and many times, its difficult to type on. Would also like the option to book a focus space more than once per day.
The Pulse location overall is great! Just a few minor issues.
Would love if this location has more options such as treadmills and vending machines in the pulse point and more areas for collaboration.

I don't understand the reasoning for having us go back in. I have been working from home since 2010. No one from my team lives in the same state as me. There is no one to collaborate with when I am here. I am literally doing the same thing I do at home that I do in the office. There is zero benefit to my work productivity by going into the office.
Please consider replacing the beverage vending machine. Abnormal amount of down time.
I normal appear in office around 6AM. I try to get in before most people arrive to keep my work as discretionate as possible and to complete as much as I can without distraction.

Working from home provides a better overall experience, allowing me to be more productive while eliminating unnecessary commute time. Even when working in the office, most of my day is still spent in Teams meetings because other associates are not in the office on the same days. This limits opportunities for in-person collaboration and defeats the purpose of being onsite. I feel that working remotely allows me to use my time more efficiently and maintain a higher level of productivity.
This creates an unnecessary hinderance to getting work completed.

While I’ve mentioned several areas where I think the office could improve, there are also things I genuinely appreciate about the new location. The view of the Arch, the Christmas tree during the holidays, the fireplace on the 10th floor, and the expanded snack and drink options are all nice additions. One perk I would love to see is a Fourth of July fireworks viewing event from the office. With the location and views we have, it feels like a great opportunity to offer something special to associates who regularly come into the office. I understand there may be limitations on guests or building access, so I think this could specifically be a perk for associates who consistently work onsite. For example, signup could be limited to associates who come into the office at least four times per month, rather than being a manager-only event or something opened to everyone. It would be a nice way to recognize and offer an added benefit to the employees who regularly utilize the office. I also really miss event parking from the previous office. Even if free event parking isn't possible, discounted parking for downtown events would be a great perk for associates who regularly work onsite.

comment: I try to make the most of my time in the office and collaborate with others but overall it makes it much harder to get work done.

I would love if someone was assigned to help build our PulsePoint community with mixers, activities and informal events. Today, most people at my PulsePoint sit at a cubicle on calls the whole time they are there, and then I can tell most people minimize the time they have to spend at the office - they leave at lunch or early to beat traffic. Even having one friend at the office can be a gamechanger. Because I don't work directly with anyone who is assigned at my PulsePoint, I don't know 95% of the people sitting around me. There's rarely a natural opportunity to introduce myself and chat. A community manager would be great. The other thing I want to raise is that the requirement to go into the office has a direct impact on our financial well-being. There's no public transit that goes to this location - I have to drive, fill my car with gas, insure it, maintain it, and the miles I am on the road just to go to the office are responsible for most of the miles on my car. The financial cost is real, and was never acknowledged. A centrally located downtown office would be a pleasure to work at and would eliminate a lot of what I dislike and find burdensome about our PulsePoint.

comment: None to note.

My overall happiness with the PulsePoint is 90% the other 10% would be improved if only the 1st floor could be updated to more modern ergonomic desks/chairs that support sit/stand and higher walls for call privacy or at least some call noice buffering. We have the options of requesting a sit/stand desk riser, but the amount of space that takes up is just not needed if we could get sit/stand cubicle desks. Or maybe just a section of updated cubicles for those that have assigned desks and are here 5 days per week to make it more comfortable to work in the office.

comment: I have a lot of meetings and it's hard to book rooms since there is a limitation on the number of times i can book a room

My location is nice and clean, which is wonderful. I greatly appreciate that. The issue I really have is that it is not necessary for me to be in where I do not interact with practically anyone. I'm a caregiver for multiple people and the requirement to come into the building so many times a week increases my stress and reduces my work-live balance considerably.
Would appreciate some light snacks in the break room as well as decaf coffee (all options are caffeinated).

It's frustrating to have to go in (even 1 or 2 days a week) for absolutely no reason. I have no team coworkers at my PulsePoint, there is zero collaboration. All it does, honestly, is waste my time and make my job harder.
Why is it always so cold in the building??

I need to come in 1 day/week, but I work best from home. I have documented instances of having to modify reservations or relocate as a result. Better reservation oversight would improve availability. **Furniture and Cleanliness:** Many chairs are stained, worn, or ergonomically inadequate, causing discomfort during an eight-hour workday. Cleaning is inconsistent, and disinfectant wipes are frequently unavailable, requiring me to bring my own supplies. **Lighting and Health Impact:** The excessively bright overhead lighting is a significant health concern. Since transitioning to Hybrid 1, my migraine frequency has increased substantially, as documented by my medical provider. The lighting contributes to these migraines, impacting my health, concentration, and productivity. Adjustable lighting or lower-light workspaces would help. **Noise and Disruptions:** The open-concept layout creates distractions, particularly when new hires gather in the central café area during training. Loud conversations disrupt associates working and participating in stakeholder calls. Utilizing the former first-floor cafeteria for training breaks would minimize these disruptions. While I understand the emphasis on onsite collaboration, the workplace should support associates' health, comfort, and productivity. Addressing these concerns would significantly improve the PulsePoint experience.

Overall, my PulsePoint experience has not met expectations. As I’ve shared, the experience is not satisfactory, and the intended gains in productivity and leader collaboration are not occurring. Based on how we work today, I do not believe the current model will deliver those outcomes. That said, I did find value in being in the office one day per week when it was planned and purposeful. I could block my schedule to avoid meetings, focus on work that was well-suited to an office setting, and collaborate with other leaders who approached it the same way. I also believe it’s important to offer constructive alternatives. If the goal is meaningful leader connection and cross-functional collaboration, I believe that would be better achieved through structured, dedicated opportunities—such as leadership summits and periodic in-person convenings—where leaders are intentionally pulled away from day-to-day work to engage, build relationships, and collaborate. Similarly, targeted travel to meet and work with the leaders we partner with regularly would likely deliver more value than increased reliance on office attendance. Pre-COVID, when teams were largely co-located and worked differently, the office environment supported collaboration more naturally. Today, with virtual and geographically dispersed teams, the current PulsePoint setup is not conducive to how leaders and teams operate. In my view, it limits leaders’ effectiveness, which in turn impacts our teams—and ultimately the experience we deliver to members.

In contrast, working remotely allows me to remain at my workstation, respond more quickly to issues, and work without unnecessary interruptions. Additionally, my role frequently involves discussions involving associates, providers, and protected health information. Maintaining privacy and confidentiality is more manageable in a dedicated home office environment than in a shared office setting. I also have significant concerns regarding personal safety and wellbeing. Traveling to and from a downtown location, parking in a garage, and walking to the building creates anxiety related to traffic, personal security, and public safety concerns. These factors have a direct impact on my overall wellbeing and ability to focus on my work. Given that my team is fully remote and not located within my geographic area, I do not see a business justification for requiring in-office attendance for my position. A fully remote work arrangement better supports productivity, confidentiality, effective leadership, and overall job performance.

A few improvements to help the productivity and experience in a pulsepoint (especially the smaller ones like Iselin) 1. More enclosed rooms with monitors and proper workspaces for Teams calls would be helpful, especially for our days which are typically full of virtual meetings where small phone booths aren't ideal. 2. A little more spacing between desks would also help reduce noise and distractions, given how many people are on calls on their headphones throughout the day. 3. Having more snack and food options would be a good especially for employees with back-to-back meetings and limited time for breaks. 4. More regular cleaning of shared desks, keyboards, and workstations would also help, as leftover food crumbs and hair can sometimes make the spaces feel dirty and unsanitary for the next person. 5. Have a way to contact someone if you forget your badge when going to the restroom or out to get food - there is no one in my team to call to let you back in and it's not allowed to let a stranger in without a badge. There must a be a way to solve for that.

comment: When we first began reporting to the Costa Mesa PulsePoint location, the initial weeks involved becoming familiar with the office environment and getting to know other employees who regularly worked onsite. Over time, we began seeing familiar faces on similar days, which naturally created opportunities to connect with colleagues across different teams and business units. These interactions eventually led to the creation of a our MS Teams group chat called “Costa Mesa Officemates,” which serves as an informal way to communicate, share information, and support one another. Through this group, we have also organized occasional activities, such as birthday celebrations and holiday potlucks. What has contributed positively to my overall PulsePoint experience is the sense of community that has developed organically among employees from different business units/teams. These connections have helped create a more familiar and supportive office environment. Although a relatively small group of us continues to take the initiative to organize opportunities to gather and connect, it has been encouraging to see our “Costa Mesa Officemates” community gradually grow. We hope to continue building on these connections and encouraging more colleagues to participate and feel included in the office community. Overall, the opportunity to build relationships and connect with colleagues beyond our immediate teams has been a positive aspect of the PulsePoint experience.
